endorsements.quote: We suggest that faculties invest in secure digital “sandboxes” and simulated EHRs that embed AI decision support tools.

Studies on automation bias—the tendency to overtrust automated recommendations—show persistent risk of overreliance on algorithms, underrecognition of new forms of error, and diffusion of responsibility when decision support systems are introduced [ 7 12 13 ].

unlisted_practices: Appoint at least one clinical AI lead with protected time at every medical school to coordinate AI teaching and supervision.
Integrate AI oversight skills into existing faculty development programs for clinical teachers.
Ensure each core clerkship has access to at least one AI-literate supervisor.
Integrate AI learning longitudinally throughout undergraduate medical curricula rather than confining it to stand-alone electives.
Coordinate shared, cloud-based AI sandboxes through national digital health partnerships to ensure equitable access across medical schools.
Accrediting bodies should articulate AI competency expectations for graduates and require evidence of a longitudinal AI learning thread and AI-related faculty development.
Licensing bodies should revise examination objectives and blueprint AI literacy, equity, and data governance content into written examinations and OSCE stations.
Develop entrustable professional activities requiring safe, supervised use of AI tools in clinical decision-making.
Examining bodies should adopt rapid-cycle blueprint reviews to keep AI assessment current.
Include Indigenous-led teaching on data sovereignty and AI, co-designed with Indigenous organizations, in medical curricula.
Redesign assessment formats easily outsourced to generative AI to reflect individual competence and uphold academic integrity.
Recognize AI-focused teaching, mentoring, and curriculum reform in faculty promotion and merit processes.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/framework paper proposing a 3-lever concurrent implementation framework for medical AI education and curriculum reform.
